passage: I'm Imran, on the web team. In the second week I noticed Kiran at the whiteboard with a tangle of arrows between tasks. The mobile screens depended on the API. So did our web pages. Kiran drew the longest chain in red: API contract, then mobile and web side by side, then integration, then release. "If the contract slips, everything behind it slips," Kiran said, and booked a two-hour session with both teams that week. We argued over field names, dates and error messages, and by Friday the contract was written down and shared. Mobile and web started work on the same Monday. I can't tell whether Kiran had done this before. It only looked obvious afterwards.

qa.q: What did Kiran book with both teams that week?
qa.a: Kiran booked a two-hour session with both teams.

qa.q: What was Kiran probably worried about when drawing the red chain?
qa.a: Kiran was probably worried that a slipped contract would hold up everything behind it.

qa.q: What else could Kiran do to protect the plan, and why?
qa.a: Kiran could make sure nobody changes the contract without telling both teams, because a quiet change could break the work already started.

qa.q: How might the mobile team have seen the early session?
qa.a: The mobile team probably felt relieved that their work would not be stuck waiting, since the contract was settled before either team began building.

grounding: Illustrates a lead seeing that one contract blocks two teams and settling it early with both, so the longest chain of dependent tasks is not delayed.

subtype: Approach: critical path thinking about dependent tasks [Thinking]
passage:
Week one. Himani, leading her first project, drew every task on a whiteboard with arrows. She stared at it. "The mobile app needs the API. The web app needs the API. The API contract isn't written." Every long chain started at the same box. "If this slips, everything slips."
So she called both teams into one room on Wednesday. Parveen led mobile; another lead ran web. "Nobody leaves until we agree what the API sends and receives." It took six hours and three rounds of chai.
Week three. With the contract fixed, mobile and web built in parallel against the same document. Parveen's team finished the login screens early.
Week seven. The backend team changed an internal detail but kept the contract the same. Neither app broke. At the demo, the client asked how the two apps stayed in sync. Himani pointed to the dog-eared contract on her desk.

qa.q: How long did the API contract meeting take?
qa.a: It took six hours and three rounds of chai.

qa.q: What was Himani thinking as she stared at the whiteboard, and how did she feel?
qa.a: She was worried and alert, realising that if the API contract slipped, everything else would slip too.

qa.q: What else could Himani do to protect the critical chain?
qa.a: She could set a clear process for changing the contract, so any change is agreed by both teams before it breaks anything.

qa.q: How might Parveen see the long Wednesday meeting afterwards?
qa.a: Parveen probably found it tiring at the time, but later glad, since the fixed contract let mobile finish early.

grounding: Shows a lead seeing that the API contract blocks both mobile and web work and finalising it with both teams in the first week.

subtype: Approach: critical path thinking about dependent tasks [Thinking]
passage:
"Ojas, you're asking why I, Ganga, fuss so much about the first week of a project. It's because of my first lead role, at twenty-five.
We were building a bank's app for both phones and web. On day two I drew all the tasks and their arrows on chart paper and spread it on the floor of my flat. And I saw it: the phone team and the web team both needed the API contract, the list of what data goes back and forth. Neither could build much without it. And it didn't exist yet.
So that was the longest chain, the one that decides the finish date. Everything else could wait a few days. That couldn't.
I put both teams in a room on day four and we wrote the contract together. People grumbled. But after that, both teams worked side by side, and nobody sat waiting.
Find the chain everything hangs from, Ojas, and settle it first."

qa.q: Where did Ganga spread the chart paper?
qa.a: On the floor of Ganga's flat.

qa.q: How did young Ganga feel on seeing the missing API contract?
qa.a: Ganga felt alarmed and focused, realising neither team could build much without it.

qa.q: What was the key choice in Ganga's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Getting both teams to write the contract on day four was the key choice, because it unblocked the longest chain of work.

qa.q: How might the two teams have felt during that day-four meeting?
qa.a: They likely felt impatient and grumbled, but later relieved that nobody had to sit waiting.

grounding: Shows a lead finding that the API contract blocks both mobile and web work and settling it with both teams in the first week.
